2.text: KETTLE. — The old women still have a vivid recollection of the clay

3.text: kettles which were used in former times, and two of these were made for

4.text: me, — one in Mariinsky Post (Fig. 104, b), and the other in Indian Point.

5.text: They are similar in shape to the soapstone kettles of the American Eskimo,¹

6.text: except that the clay walls are necessarily thicker and clumsier. Some clay

7.text: kettles from St. Lawrence Island, also of the same shape, are among the

8.text: collections of the National Museum in Washington. Some fragments which

9.text: I found on Baron Korff’s Bay demonstrate that the Koryak of the Pacific

10.text: coast must have used similar kettles. Some of these fragments have the

11.text: same texture as the Chukchee kettles described above. The others, as well

12.text: as some fragments from the ancient “jaw-bone houses” of the Asiatic Eskimo,

15.text: The kettles and the lamps of my collection are not baked. When being

16.text: manufactured, they are covered with a coating of reindeer or seal blood,

17.text: sometimes mixed with ochre, and well dried before the fire. After this they

18.text: are filled with oil and left to stand for several days, during which time the

19.text: oil penetrates the pores of the clay. This makes the kettle less brittle.

20.text: In ancient times the kettles and some of the lamps may have been baked.
